extracted.intended_audience: aspiring writers (especially young-adult/teen authors) and fans of John Green
extracted.subtask_short: writing advice for aspiring YA authors
extracted.subtask_description: An interview-style set of craft and career guidelines for writers (particularly those working in or aspiring to write young-adult fiction). Covers reading, discipline, revision, mentorship, finding structure, use of autobiographical material, publishing/adaptation experiences, and career mindset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read a lot / apprenticeship by reading
rubrics_metrics.description: "Reading is the only apprenticeship we have."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading widely provides the record of techniques and 'tricks' that let you create experiences in readers' minds; steal/learn from other authors. Use reading as practical training rather than theoretical instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show up / discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: "You have to show up. You have to have discipline and you have to keep going." (father's advice: 'coal miners don't get coal miner’s block')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat writing as work rather than waiting for inspiration; persist through writer's block by maintaining routine and output. The admonition implies regular practice is non-negotiable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find and keep a mentor or writing group
rubrics_metrics.description: You need somebody (mentor, agent, writing group) who can 'shepherd you through the process.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentors/editors can spot publishable potential and help develop drafts. Having people who'll give iterative feedback (as Ilene Cooper did) is critical to turning possibility into publishable work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revise extensively / long revision process
rubrics_metrics.description: Spent years re-writing drafts (e.g., three years revising Looking for Alaska).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect prolonged revision cycles; initial drafts may show 'moments of possibility' but require extensive editing. Rewriting is central to craft; don't expect a publishable book on first completion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure can be discovered during drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: Often you 'discover' structure in the writing process rather than planning it fully in advance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open to non-linear drafting and to later reorganizing (e.g., turning a non-chronological draft into a deliberately structured midpoint device). 'A-ha' moments of structure often arise after sustained work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use time/temporal devices thoughtfully
rubrics_metrics.description: Using devices like '83 days before'/'26 days after' or framing narrative around major events (pre/post 9/11) to construct time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructing time around meaningful events can give narrative shape. Consider dating, non-chronological sequencing, or midpoint devices to reinforce thematic and emotional stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use autobiographical material selectively and transform it
rubrics_metrics.description: Books may be rooted in real experiences, but over time become less autobiographical; characters often are composites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It's acceptable to base aspects on real life ('the character Alaska...is really a composite'), but use fiction's conventions to obscure and reshape personal material for story and privacy reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscure personal elements when necessary (privacy/publicity awareness)
rubrics_metrics.description: After increased public exposure (e.g., YouTube), the author wanted to 'use the conventions of fiction to obscure' his experiences and maintain privacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of how public activity affects what you can/should put into fiction; fictionalize to protect privacy or to serve the story's needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create a guide/chorus voice but disguise it
rubrics_metrics.description: If you need a Greek-chorus-like guide (to separate story levels), make that figure distinct and unlikable enough to avoid straightforward authorial commentary (Van Houten example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using metafictional or explanatory voices, ensure they function dramatically and do not read as author surrogate; craft them to sort levels of story without simplifying interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer simplicity when complexity is gratuitous
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid making problems complex for no reason; a simple solution (as offered by screenwriters) can be better than forced complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be willing to simplify plot solutions; complexity should add thematic or emotional thickness, not exist because the author couldn't find a simpler choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be open to outside solutions and collaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Screenwriters sometimes solve problems for the novelist; being open to that can improve the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collaboration (e.g., in adaptations) can resolve narrative issues the author couldn't. Evaluate outside input on its merits rather than rejecting it for being external.

rubrics_metrics.name: Push back on unnecessary sacrifices in adaptations but stay involved
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors may need to object to compromises made for movie narrative, but inclusion in conversations helps preserve the book's vision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage with adaptation teams, voice concerns about unnecessary changes, and seek to be part of the process to protect core themes/vision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry engagement and networking matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Working in the book world and building relationships helped; 'networking matters' — mentors and contacts can open doors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put yourself in literary contexts (magazines, events); relationships can lead to introductions and opportunities, even if talent is primary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept career-long variability; value longevity over spikes
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for a long career where 'half of them are bad'; prefer sustained output rather than a single meteoric success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set expectations that not every book will be a masterpiece; cultivate persistence and a long-term view of creative output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn from flawed works; value ambition and risk
rubrics_metrics.description: There is value in books with big flaws because they demonstrate ambition and a writer at work (Vonnegut example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't only read or produce 'masterpieces'—engage with works that take risks; they offer learning opportunities and models of experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persist despite early discouragement or setbacks
rubrics_metrics.description: Not making advanced classes or being 'not the best writer in my high school' didn't stop the author from returning to stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early failure or rejection is not definitive; keep writing and returning to stories despite discouragement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let published books stand (resist changing them post-publication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once books are in readers' hands, the author feels he doesn't have the right to change them; their weaknesses and strengths remain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat publication as a boundary; accept that the published text belongs to readers and be cautious about revising for later comfort or impulse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write the books you loved reading early on
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim to write the kinds of books you loved when you were younger (Green: 'I want to write the kind of books that I loved when I was in high school').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let formative reading preferences inform your voice and thematic interests; authenticity of attraction to material can guide sustained creative effort.
